A.explanation: The ampere, unit of electric current, is one of the seven SI base units.

B.explanation: The coulomb is a derived unit for charge, since $Q = It$ gives $1 \text{ C} = 1 \text{ A s}$.

C.explanation: Degree Celsius is not an SI base unit; the SI base unit for thermodynamic temperature is the kelvin.

D.explanation: Gram is not the SI base unit for mass; the SI base unit is the kilogram.

hints: Identify what quantity each listed unit measures: ampere for electric current, coulomb for charge, degree Celsius for temperature, and gram for mass.
Recall the SI base quantities include electric current, mass and thermodynamic temperature, with base units kilogram for mass and kelvin for temperature.
Test for a derived unit by checking if it can be built from other units, such as charge from current and time using $Q = It$ to give $\text{C} = \text{A s}$.
walkthrough: List the idea of SI base units: seven independent units including metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela, from which all other SI units are derived.
Check ampere: it is the defined SI base unit for electric current and cannot be broken into other base units.
Check coulomb: from $Q = It$, charge has unit $1 \text{ C} = 1 \text{ A s}$, so it is a derived unit made from ampere and second.
Check degree Celsius and gram: temperature has SI base unit kelvin, not degree Celsius, and mass has SI base unit kilogram, not gram.
Only ampere meets the definition of an SI base unit. This is option A.
